docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: Some APIs require authentication (a way to prove who you are). JSONPlaceholder doesn’t need it, but here’s a simple example you might see in real APIs.

docs.title: API Key example
docs.text:
Some APIs give you a key like this:

12345-ABCDE-SECRET

You include it in your request header: ```bash curl -s https://api.example.com/data \ -H "Authorization: Bearer 12345-ABCDE-SECRET"

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text: APIs return status codes and messages. Use this page to understand common errors and what to do next.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Status Meaning What you should do 200 OK All good 201 Created Resource created 400 Bad Request Fix your JSON or query parameters 401 Unauthorized Add/refresh your API key or token 403 Forbidden You don’t have permission 404 Not Found Check the URL or resource ID 429 Too Many Requests Slow down; add retry/backoff 500 Server Error Try again later; capture request details

docs.title: Example: 404 Not Found
docs.text:
Requesting a user that doesn’t exist: ```bash curl -i https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/9999 HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found curl -s https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users | head curl -s -X POST https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "title": 123 }' # title should be a string curl -s -X POST https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "title": "Hello", "body": "First post", "userId": 1 }'

Reply “done” when saved, and I’ll give you the one-line change to add it to your menu.

docs.title: Getting Started with the Example API
docs.text: This guide gets you from zero to a working request in under 2 minutes using the free JSONPlaceholder API. It’s perfect for demonstrating API calls and documentation skills—no sign-up or API key required.

docs.title: Quickstart (60 seconds)
docs.text:
1. Base URL https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/?utm_source=chatgpt.com

  2. Read data (GET) ```bash curl -s https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1

Expected response (shortened):

{ "id": 1, "name": "Leanne Graham", "email": "Sincere@april.biz" }

  1. Create data (POST)

curl -s -X POST https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"title":"Hello","body":"First post","userId":1}'

Expected response:

{ "title": "Hello", "body": "First post", "userId": 1, "id": 101 }

docs.title: How Mobile Payments Work: NFC + Tokenization
docs.text: When you tap your phone to pay, your real card number is not sent. Instead, a token (a safe stand-in number) is used.

docs.title: Step 1 — Your phone stores a token
docs.text:
• Your bank/card network creates a token that represents your real card.
  • The token lives in a secure part of your device (called the “secure element”).

docs.title: Step 2 — Tap with NFC
docs.text:
• NFC allows your phone and the payment terminal to communicate at close range.
  • Your phone sends the token + a one-time cryptogram (like a digital fingerprint).

docs.title: Step 3 — Authorization
docs.text:
• The terminal sends the token to the payment network.
  • The network swaps the token for your real card behind the scenes and asks your bank: “Approve this purchase?”

docs.title: Step 4 — Response
docs.text:
• Bank approves or declines.
  • The result flows back through the payment network to the merchant.
  • You see Approved on your phone or the terminal.

docs.title: Why tokenization matters
docs.text:
• Merchants never see or store your real card number.
  • If a hacker steals the token, it’s useless outside that specific device.
  • This greatly reduces fraud risk.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Mobile payments combine: - NFC for fast, wireless communication - Tokenization for safety - Cryptograms for transaction security

Result: payments that are quick, secure, and private.

docs.title: Tutorial: Make Your First API Call in 5 Minutes
docs.text: This tutorial walks you through calling the JSONPlaceholder API. By the end, you’ll have made your first real API request.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A computer with curl installed (Mac and Linux have it by default).
  • Internet connection.

docs.title: Step 1 — Open your terminal
docs.text: On Mac: Applications → Utilities → Terminal. You’ll see a prompt like this: juelmahoney@Juels-Air ~ %

docs.title: Step 2 — Try a simple request
docs.text:
Run this command: ```bash curl -s https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1

Expected response (shortened):

{ "userId": 1, "id": 1, "title": "sunt aut facere repellat provident occaecati", "body": "quia et suscipit..." }

docs.title: Step 3 — Create your own resource
docs.text:
Use POST to create a fake post:

curl -s -X POST https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"title":"My First Post","body":"Hello world!","userId":1}'

Expected response:

"title": "My First Post", "body": "Hello world!", "userId": 1, "id": 101

docs.title: Step 4 — Explore further
docs.text:
Now that you can send GET and POST requests, try experimenting:

  • Change the title or body values in your POST request.
  • Explore different endpoints like /users or /comments.
  • Try combining commands, for example:

```bash curl -s https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1

Expected response (shortened):

{ "id": 1, "name": "Leanne Graham", "email": "Sincere@april.biz" }
